To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the COBE-DMRA 53 and 9 GHz 4 year sky maps have a significant contribution to their anisotropy which is not Gaussian and which is not correlated with the diffuse Galactic emission as seen by the DIRBE and Haslam experiments.
the CMB anisotropic sky is not Gaussian and that the dominant non-Gaussianity is found at the multipole of $\ell=16$.
the 53 and 70 GHz COBE-DRM 4 year maps show evidence for non-Gaussian anisotropy and that the dominant effect is located in the multipole range $\ell \sim 16$.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (1) How to construct a goodness-of-fit test for non-Gaussian CMB anisotropic maps; (2) What is the best way to estimate the normalized bispectrum; (3) What are the systematics of the bispectrum estimator?
the following questions: (i) Is the CMB anisotropic?
the study of the distribution of the normalized bispectrum estimator, which is a statistic for testing the Gaussian hypothesis in the CMB anisotropic maps.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a strong indication for the existence of primordial non-Gaussianity, and that this effect may have been detected in the COBE-DMRs 53 and 94 GHz 4 year maps.
the 53 and 91 GHz COBE-4yr maps are consistent with non-Gaussianity, but that we are unable to rule out Gaussianity at high confidence level.
the COBE-DMRA anisotropy data are inconsistent with a Gaussian distribution at the confidence level of 98% (95% if the systematics are taken into account).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CMB anisotropic signal is non-Gaussian at the confidence level of $\sim 98\%$ and the non-Gaussianity is dominated by the contribution from multipoles of order $\sim 16$.
the CMB anisotropic signal is non-Gaussian and its origin is unknown.
we have demonstrated the presence of non-Gaussianity on a scale of 10$^o$ in the CMB anisotropic maps.
The main takeaway from our work is that

non-Gaussianity is a robust and potentially powerful tool for the detection of foreground contamination in CMB maps, as well as the detection and characterization of primordial non-Gaussianity itself.
the bispectrum is a powerful probe of non-Gaussianity, and it can be used as a diagnostic for the presence of foregrounds.
non-Gaussianity is an essential feature of the CMB anisotropic signal.
